reviewBoundary: Three complete adult reading practices, two five-question passages for each CET tier and one six-question longer C1 essay. Fictional cases, qualified general discussion, all evidence/options reviewed by same author, no independent calibration.

units.title: A shared recipe and a different route
units.alignmentNote: Complete original written-reading practice following the referenced two-passage/five-question or single-passage/six-question response structure. Source is a level/family reference only.

materials.title: The recipe with a margin
materials.text:
When a neighbourhood group decided to collect recipes, its organisers expected a neat list of ingredients and instructions from each household. The first contributions were less tidy. One recipe said to use a small cup without naming its size. Another told the cook to continue until the mixture felt right. A third included a story about the person who had taught the writer to make the dish.

At the first meeting, a volunteer suggested removing everything except standard measurements and numbered steps. That would make the collection easier to use, but some contributors worried that it would erase what made their recipe theirs. The group had to decide whether it was making a practical cookbook, a record of local lives or something that could do both.

They tested two recipes with cooks who had not seen them before. The unfamiliar cooks asked useful questions. What kind of flour? How full was the cup? Was the pan covered? These questions showed where a confident family habit did not automatically become a clear written instruction.

The organisers invited the contributors to answer those questions rather than silently filling the gaps themselves. They added a separate margin for memories and variations. The main instructions could then be made usable without pretending that the dish had only one family history or one possible version.

Not every contributor agreed to the same changes. One preferred a short personal account rather than a usable recipe, and it appeared in a different section. The finished collection made those differences visible.

Its success did not come from making every page identical. It came from explaining what each page offered. A reader looking for tonight's dinner could find tested instructions; a reader interested in neighbourhood stories could explore the margins and accounts. Clear structure allowed both purposes to remain, instead of requiring one to disappear.

questions.prompt: What difficulty appears in the first submissions?
options: Some instructions depend on unspoken household knowledge
Every contributor refuses to give ingredients
All recipes use identical measured cups
None includes any personal history
questions.explanation: Cup size and feel rely on tacit knowledge. Ingredients exist and stories/varied measures are included.

questions.prompt: What concern follows the proposal to remove extra material?
options: Nobody will be allowed to cook
Every recipe will become dangerous automatically
Printing will become impossible
Personal connections may be lost
questions.explanation: Contributors fear erasing what makes recipes theirs. Automatic danger/impossibility/cooking prohibition are not claimed.

questions.prompt: Why involve unfamiliar cooks?
options: They guarantee that every recipe tastes identical
They eliminate the need for any written instructions
They reveal questions experienced family cooks may overlook
They replace all contributors as authors
questions.explanation: Their questions expose missing explicit details. They do not ensure uniform taste, seize authorship or remove instructions.

questions.prompt: How are missing details resolved?
options: Every incomplete page is destroyed
Contributors are asked rather than gaps being invented silently
Organisers guess without recording any change
Only the stories are retained
questions.explanation: The organisers ask contributors and keep both instructions and narrative. Guessing/destruction/stories-only are contradicted.

questions.prompt: What makes the final collection usable for two purposes?
options: Making every page exactly the same
A structure that identifies instructions, memories and other accounts
Removing all variation from family dishes
Claiming every personal account is a tested recipe
questions.explanation: Separate margins/sections identify purposes. Uniformity/erased variation/false testing claims undermine that clarity.

materials.title: The route that changed with the hour
materials.text:
I used to choose my walk to work by comparing distances on a map. The shorter route passed a busy delivery yard; the longer one followed a canal. Since I wanted to arrive quickly, the short route seemed obviously better.

For several weeks, I reached the yard at the same time as its morning deliveries. Lorries turned slowly across the pavement, and staff directed people around the entrance. The interruptions were properly managed, but they meant that the distance saved on the map did not always save time on the ground.

One day I left home earlier and crossed the same place before deliveries began. The walk was quiet and direct. I realised that I had been comparing routes as fixed lines while ignoring the hour at which I used them.

I kept a simple record for a week: departure time, route and arrival time. I did not treat it as a scientific study of everyone in the town. It described my own journeys under a limited set of conditions. Still, it helped me notice that the canal path was often more predictable during the delivery period.

Predictability mattered because I sometimes had to open our office. Arriving at roughly the expected time was more useful on those days than occasionally achieving the shortest possible walk. On other mornings, I could choose the direct route and allow extra time if necessary.

I had not discovered a single best path. I had learned to ask a more useful question: best for which journey, at which time and for what purpose? The map still mattered, but it did not contain the whole experience of walking. Combining its information with a modest record of actual trips made my choices better informed, without pretending that a week's observations guaranteed next month's conditions.

questions.prompt: Why does the shorter route sometimes fail to save time?
options: Morning deliveries interrupt passage at the yard
The narrator refuses all managed crossings
The map has no distances marked
The canal closes every morning
questions.explanation: Delivery vehicles create managed delays. Missing map distances/canal closure/refusal are not stated.

questions.prompt: What does leaving earlier reveal?
options: Every delivery has been cancelled permanently
The canal path is always the only safe option
The same route can function differently at another hour
Distance never matters to walking
questions.explanation: Earlier timing avoids deliveries. It does not establish permanent cancellation, exclusive safety or distance irrelevance.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator describe the week’s record?
options: A replacement for every map
A limited account of personal journeys
A universal scientific conclusion about all residents
A guarantee about future months
questions.explanation: The record is explicitly personal/limited with no future guarantee. It complements the map.

questions.prompt: Why is predictability useful on some days?
options: The narrator wants every walk to last exactly an hour
The yard requires payment for walking
The canal path has no exit
The narrator must open the office
questions.explanation: Opening the office gives a reliable-arrival purpose. Fixed-hour walking/payment/no exit are invented.

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the narrator reach?
options: The shortest line is always best
One good week settles every future choice
Maps should no longer be used
Route choice should consider time, purpose and observed conditions
questions.explanation: The conclusion integrates conditions with map information. It rejects an automatic distance rule and permanent certainty.

units.title: Meeting records and travelling seeds
units.alignmentNote: Complete original written-reading practice following the referenced two-passage/five-question or single-passage/six-question response structure. Source is a level/family reference only.

materials.title: What meeting minutes leave open
materials.text:
A set of meeting minutes can look like a complete account because it is official, dated and arranged under numbered headings. Yet minutes usually serve a narrower function: they record matters such as decisions, actions and responsibilities. They are not necessarily a transcript of every remark, nor a map of everything every participant thought.

This distinction matters when a reader tries to reconstruct a disagreement months later. A minute stating that a proposal was approved may establish the recorded decision. It may say little about the range of views expressed before that decision, especially if the organisation's practice is to summarise outcomes rather than attribute individual comments.

Silence in the document therefore needs interpretation. The absence of a named objection does not automatically prove that nobody objected. It may reflect the recording convention, the level of detail chosen or an omission. Equally, it would be unreasonable to invent an objection merely because the minutes are brief. The evidence supports some claims more strongly than others.

A useful record makes its own status clear. Draft minutes may still be corrected; approved minutes carry a different procedural standing. An action marked complete should not be confused with an action merely assigned. Dates, version labels and responsibility names help readers understand which stage a document represents.

Corrections also need a visible route. If an error about a decision is found, quietly replacing the text can leave earlier readers relying on a superseded account. An organisation may instead issue a correction or approve revised minutes, following its rules. The appropriate process depends on the setting, but the need to distinguish versions remains.

For participants, good minutes can support practical cooperation. Someone who missed the meeting can identify the task they own and the deadline agreed. Someone reviewing progress can ask whether an action occurred rather than reopening every conversation that preceded it. These are substantial benefits, even though the document does not preserve the entire event.

For later researchers, the same record may become one source among others. Agendas, drafts, correspondence and accounts from participants can help answer questions that the minutes were not designed to settle. Their value lies partly in being a particular kind of record. Treating them as either total truth or worthless summary misses the more careful possibility: use the document for what it can establish, and identify what further evidence would be needed for the rest.

questions.prompt: What is the central distinction in the opening?
options: Numbered headings prove exact speech is preserved
An official outcome record is not necessarily a complete transcript
Every official document contains all private thoughts
Minutes have no practical purpose
questions.explanation: The opening distinguishes minutes’ function from exhaustive speech/thought. Official form does not ensure completeness and practical purpose is substantial.

questions.prompt: What can absence of a named objection establish by itself?
options: That all participants privately agreed
That a hidden objection definitely occurred
Neither that no objection existed nor that one must be invented
That the recorded decision was never made
questions.explanation: The third paragraph rejects both absence-as-proof and invention. It does not erase the decision.

questions.prompt: Why are version labels useful?
options: They make corrections permanently impossible
They reveal every speaker’s intention
They identify procedural status and stages of action
They turn every draft into an approved record
questions.explanation: Draft/approved and assigned/completed stages differ. Labels do not confer approval, ban correction or reveal minds.

questions.prompt: What risk is associated with silently replacing an erroneous text?
options: All earlier readers instantly receive the correction
Earlier readers may continue relying on a superseded version
The original meeting automatically happens again
Every task is necessarily cancelled
questions.explanation: The correction paragraph names earlier reliance. No automatic notification, repeated meeting or universal cancellation follows.

questions.prompt: How should later researchers approach minutes?
options: As substitutes for checking any other source
As summaries with no evidential value
As documents that settle every possible question
As useful records whose limits may require other evidence
questions.explanation: The final paragraph advocates specific evidence plus complementary sources. Total truth/uselessness/source replacement are rejected.

materials.title: A seed’s journey is not a promise
materials.text:
A winged seed spinning away from a tree can invite a simple story: the plant has sent its offspring to a new home. The image is useful, provided we remember what it leaves out. Movement away from the parent is only one stage. Landing, germination and later survival depend on conditions that a brief flight does not guarantee.

Dispersal can take many forms. Some seeds travel with wind; others move through water or with animals. Structures associated with those routes differ, and a familiar example should not become a rule for every species. Nor does a structure tell us exactly where an individual seed will end up. Weather, obstacles and chance encounters contribute to the journey.

Distance itself is not an automatic measure of success. A seed carried far from its parent may land on a surface where it cannot grow. Another travelling only a short distance may reach suitable conditions. The relevant question is not simply how far it moved, but whether it reached a place where the next stages of its life could occur.

Observing dispersal therefore involves several linked questions. A student watching seeds fall can record direction, distance and the conditions of the observation. That record may help describe a movement pattern. It does not, without later evidence, establish how many plants will eventually grow. Counting arriving seeds and counting established seedlings are different measurements.

This difference matters when discussing a plant's spread. Finding a few seeds beyond a garden boundary is evidence of transport. It is not yet evidence of a lasting population there. Conversely, failing to notice a conspicuous flight does not prove that no dispersal occurred; some routes are less visible than a spinning wing in sunlight.

The language of travel can help us pay attention, but it should not quietly assign intention to the seed. A wing is not a ticket bought for a chosen destination, and a fruit is not a conscious negotiation with an animal. These comparisons are ways of explaining patterns, not descriptions of a plant's private plan.

A more careful account can keep the vivid image while restoring the missing stages. We can admire the turning seed, investigate the conditions that carry it and ask what happens after it lands. The journey then becomes part of a larger process rather than a complete success story compressed into a moment of flight. It is precisely by distinguishing these stages that an everyday observation can lead to more useful biological questions.

questions.prompt: What does the opening say a seed’s flight does not guarantee?
options: Successful germination and survival after landing
That all seeds have wings
That the seed moved at all
That the parent tree is visible
questions.explanation: Movement is one stage without assured later establishment. The other claims are not the stated guarantee issue.

questions.prompt: Why is distance alone inadequate as a success measure?
options: Long-distance seeds always choose their destinations
Distance cannot ever be observed
Every nearby seed necessarily dies
A distant landing may be unsuitable for growth
questions.explanation: Suitability, not distance alone, enables next stages. Nearby death, conscious choice and unobservability are rejected or unsupported.

questions.prompt: What distinction is drawn between arrivals and seedlings?
options: They measure different stages and require different evidence
They are always identical counts
Both can be known from one brief flight
Neither can ever be recorded
questions.explanation: Arrival differs from establishment. Identity, complete flight inference and impossible records are not claimed.

questions.prompt: What can finding seeds outside a garden establish?
options: Transport beyond the boundary, with establishment still unproven
That no other dispersal route exists
A permanent population in every case
A conscious plan by the plant
questions.explanation: Boundary crossing is transport evidence, not permanent establishment or intention/exclusivity.

questions.prompt: What does the author recommend about travel metaphors?
options: Use them while recognising the stages and intentions they can obscure
Assume the metaphor proves survival
Ban every vivid image from biology
Treat a wing as a consciously purchased ticket
questions.explanation: The conclusion retains the image with limits. It rejects prohibition, literal intentional tickets and compressed success claims.

units.title: Restoring a work without erasing its history
units.alignmentNote: Complete original written-reading practice following the referenced two-passage/five-question or single-passage/six-question response structure. Source is a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Which version is being restored?
materials.text:
The word restoration carries an attractive promise: something damaged or obscured will be brought back. Applied to an old film, building or painting, it can suggest that a single authentic state lies beneath later interference, waiting to be recovered. Sometimes a task does involve removing a clearly identified problem. But the promise becomes less straightforward when the object has changed repeatedly during a long life.

Consider an invented film that circulated in several edited versions. The first release was shortened for a different market; a later version replaced a piece of music; another used a new title sequence approved by the director years afterwards. A present-day team may have good reasons to reconstruct the first release. That choice does not make every later version meaningless, nor does it remove the need to explain which history the restoration is representing.

The available material may itself be mixed. One surviving print can preserve a scene missing from another but have poorer image quality. A soundtrack may exist separately from the corresponding picture. Combining sources can recover something valuable, while also producing a version that no historical audience saw in precisely that assembled form. Such a result need not be fraudulent. It does need an account of what was combined and why.

A similar question arises with visible wear. A scratch caused by accidental damage may be treated differently from a change deliberately made during a work's circulation. Yet the boundary is not always self-evident, and judgments about it belong to the restoration's argument. Calling every unwanted feature noise can conceal the fact that someone has decided which traces count as history and which count as interference.

Technical success is therefore only one part of the work. A cleaner image may make a scene easier to see, but excessive processing can also remove texture that belonged to the source. A repaired building can function better while losing evidence of earlier use. These are not reasons to reject intervention in advance. They are reasons to connect a proposed intervention with the purpose it is meant to serve and the evidence it might alter.

Documentation provides a practical response. Teams can record the source materials, the decisions taken and the limits of confidence. Where feasible, retaining earlier versions or reversible records allows later workers to revisit a judgment. The aim is not to preserve every scratch in every public presentation, nor to demand that an ordinary viewer study a technical report before enjoying a film. It is to make the work's new clarity compatible with an honest account of how that clarity was achieved.

Nor does openness require a public presentation to offer every surviving version at once. An exhibition, cinema or reading edition still needs a usable form. The distinction is between making a selection and presenting that selection as though no alternatives had existed. A main version can be accompanied by a concise explanation, with further records available for those who need them. Different levels of access can serve different audiences without turning the shortest label into a claim of complete historical certainty.

Audience expectations matter as well. A label saying restored may be read as a guarantee that the viewer is seeing exactly what the first audience saw. A more specific description can prevent that assumption without diminishing the result: reconstructed from several surviving sources, for instance, identifies a different achievement from reproducing one intact historical print. Precision in the label helps the audience appreciate the work actually done.

Restoration can thus be understood as a responsible present-day relationship with an inherited object, rather than an effortless disappearance of the present. Skill may make the intervention unobtrusive, but it cannot make choices cease to have been made. The strongest work need not claim to abolish all uncertainty. It can offer a carefully supported version, preserve the reasoning behind it and leave future readers or viewers able to ask a better question than whether the object has simply been returned to its original self.

questions.prompt: What assumption about restoration does the opening complicate?
options: That objects sometimes survive for a long time
That damage can ever be identified
That restored works may be enjoyed
That every object has one obvious authentic state ready to recover
questions.explanation: The opening questions a single recoverable state across multiple changes. It allows identifiable problems, long histories and enjoyment.

questions.prompt: What is the point of the invented film’s several versions?
options: Choosing an early release is a reasoned choice among meaningful histories
Different markets can never change a film
A director’s later approval always erases earlier evidence
Every later version is automatically a forgery
questions.explanation: The example values an early reconstruction without denying later history. Forgery/erasure/no-change universals contradict it.

questions.prompt: How does the author view combining surviving sources?
options: It removes the need to identify sources
It can be valuable if the assembly and its rationale are explained
It proves one historical audience saw exactly that assembly
It is necessarily fraudulent
questions.explanation: Combined reconstruction may never have existed intact but can be honest with documentation. Fraud/guaranteed historical viewing/no provenance are rejected.

questions.prompt: Why question the label noise for unwanted features?
options: It can hide judgments about history versus interference
It establishes that every visible trace must always remain
It proves all scratches were deliberate artistic choices
It makes technical processing impossible
questions.explanation: Noise can conceal selection judgments. The author neither treats all scratches as intentional nor bans processing/removal.

questions.prompt: What role does documentation play?
options: It guarantees that no judgment can ever change
It makes decisions and uncertainty inspectable and may support later revision
It requires every viewer to read a technical report
It replaces the restored object entirely
questions.explanation: Source/decision/confidence records support revisiting. Mandatory viewer study, immutable judgment and replacement are not its role.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the conclusion?
options: Uncertainty means restoration should never begin
Restoration is a supported present-day intervention whose choices should remain accountable
A skilled intervention contains no choices
Every restoration must recreate an uncontested original exactly
questions.explanation: The final paragraph treats accountable choice and supported versions as strengths. Choice-free skill, obligatory exact original and paralysis are rejected.
